summary:
Sarah Chieng, Head of Developer Experience at Cerebras, presents a practical playbook for adapting to ultra-fast AI code generation. Cerebras and OpenAI released Codex Spark, generating code at 1,200 tokens per second—roughly 20x faster than Sonnet and Opus families at 40-60 tokens/sec. Over the past two years, model speeds remained relatively constant at 50-150 tokens/sec while models grew smarter and context windows expanded. Codex Spark represents a new regime that fundamentally changes how developers should interact with coding models.

The speed increase results from optimization across the entire AI inference stack. At the hardware level, the memory wall is the primary bottleneck—memory movement accounts for 50-80% of inference latency. Traditional Nvidia GPUs store memory off-chip in HBM, creating bandwidth bottlenecks. Cerebras distributes SRAM across its wafer-scale processor so every core has direct access. Disaggregated inference splits prefill (compute-bound, parallel) and decode (memory-bound, sequential) onto separately optimized hardware. Model architecture optimizations include mixture of experts and REAP. At the inference optimization level, KV cache reuse avoids recalculating attention.

The current developer landscape shows risky behaviors: running six Claude Code terminals, 500+ agent swarms, or eight agents across five screens, generating massive unverified code. Chieng's playbook addresses this with model orchestration (larger models for planning, faster models for execution), continuous validation (linting, tests, diff reviews at every step), and cherrypicking (generating 75 versions across five sub-agents).

The remaining playbook items emphasize a shift to real-time collaboration: developers should treat fast models as pair programmers, actively steering them with constraints like max diff sizes and file deletion bans rather than spawning agents and walking away. Continuous refactoring becomes free at 1,200 tokens/sec. Context management is critical because compaction that previously took ten minutes now arrives in thirty seconds. Chieng recommends a four-file external memory system—agents.md, plan.md, progress.md, verify.md—so every new session picks up where prior work left off rather than starting from scratch. She concludes that faster models fundamentally improve developer experience, making good practices practical rather than miserable.

sections.title: Introduction to the impact of fast AI code generation
sections.summary: Chieng introduces the problem: developers have built bad habits around slow AI code generation—massive one-shot prompts, huge commits, multiple agents thinking simultaneously. Cerebras and OpenAI released Codex Spark at 1,200 tokens/sec, 20x faster than Sonnet/Opus at 40-60 tokens/sec. Unless habits change, these models will generate 1,200 tokens/sec of bad code.

sections.title: Historical context of model speeds
sections.summary: Over the past two years, models have gotten bigger and smarter with larger context windows, but speeds remained relatively constant at 50-150 tokens/sec across Gemini, Claude, GPT, and Sonnet families. Codex Spark is the first of many faster models, requiring a new Y-axis on speed charts.

sections.title: Why AI inference speeds are increasing
sections.summary: The entire AI inference stack is being optimized simultaneously. Hardware: the memory wall means memory movement takes 50-80% of latency; Nvidia GPUs use off-chip HBM creating bandwidth bottlenecks, while Cerebras distributes SRAM across its wafer so every core has direct access. Disaggregated inference splits prefill (compute-bound, parallel) and decode (memory-bound, sequential) onto separately optimized hardware. Model architecture: mixture of experts activates only subsets per token, and REAP prunes unused experts. Inference optimizations: KV cache reuse avoids recalculating attention.

sections.title: The current developer landscape and risks of 'slob'
sections.summary: The current internet celebrates running six Claude Code terminals, 500+ agent swarms, and eight agents across five screens. The reality is massive unverified code generation. With faster inference, this becomes increasingly dangerous, generating technical debt at unprecedented scale with no plan for handling it.

sections.title: Playbook: Orchestrating models and sub-agents
sections.summary: Speed is now a third optimization dimension alongside intelligence and cost. Use larger models like GPT 5.4 for planning and long-horizon workflows, then spawn Codex Spark sub-agents for step-by-step execution. Capture successful sessions as skills—use a larger model for the initial hard task, then have a faster agent replay the verified workflow repeatedly in the background.

sections.title: Playbook: Validation and automated testing
sections.summary: At 1,200 tokens/sec, validation becomes essentially free. There is no excuse not to run test suites, linting, pre-commit hooks, diff reviews, and browser-based QA automations at every step of the workflow, rather than only at the end or right before pushing.

sections.title: Playbook: Cherrypicking and variety in output
sections.summary: Fast models enable generating 15 versions in the time one previously took, or 75 versions across 5 sub-agents, then cherry-picking the best. This artificially induces taste into model output—useful for UI design, architecture directions, and research where variety matters.

sections.title: Playbook: Adopting a real-time collaborative mental model
sections.summary: With fast models, developers should not spawn a session and walk away. Instead, treat the model as a real-time pair programmer: sit down, ask it to collect repo context, ask how things work, and stay in the driver's seat making decisions. The AI should help make decisions, not the other way around.

sections.title: Playbook: Avoiding 'slob' and active steering
sections.summary: Rather than spawning 10 agents and never verifying, developers should run two to three sessions and actively steer the code. Be super specific: ban the model from deleting files, give it a max diff size, restrict to read/write only, and provide steering directions like 'only change this, don't touch types yet.' The developer, AI agent, and codebase should work together as a connected system.

sections.title: Playbook: Continuous refactoring
sections.summary: Like validation, continuous refactoring is basically free at 1,200 tokens/sec. Instead of cleaning up code right before committing, bake automated refactoring into the workflow after every checklist task—delete unused imports, clean up unnecessary lines, and standardize function structure automatically.

sections.title: Playbook: Context management and external memory systems
sections.summary: Context compaction that previously took 10 minutes now takes 30 seconds at 20x speed, making context management more important than ever. Chieng recommends a four-file external memory system: agents.md (define agents/subagents), plan.md (step-by-step checklist generated at the start), progress.md (tracks done/todo so new sessions pick up where prior work left off), and verify.md (ensures clean code at each step). Use larger models like GPT 5.3/5.4 Codex to create the plan, then Codex Spark executes the checklist. Chieng concludes that faster models fundamentally improve developer experience, enabling good practices without misery. Her handle is milksandmatcha.
